plainEnglish: A label takes a cut of everything you earn as an artist, not just record sales: touring, merch, sponsorships, even your publishing.
whyItHurts: You can end up paying a company that does nothing for your live shows or merch, and the cut often continues for the full term of the deal, which can be many years.
whatToDo: Ask which income streams are included and what the label will actually invest in each one.
Try to carve out touring, merch and publishing, or lower the percentage for them.
Have an entertainment lawyer read it before you sign anything.

plainEnglish: The company owns your recordings forever, not for a set number of years. You can never get them back, even if the company does nothing with them.
whyItHurts: Your masters are your biggest long-term asset. Giving them up permanently means you stop controlling licensing, re-releases and sync deals for the rest of your life.
whatToDo: Ask for a license instead of an ownership transfer.
If ownership transfers, ask for a reversion clause: the rights return to you after a fixed number of years or if sales stop.
Never sign a perpetual deal as a rushed favor or a quick cash grab.
lookFor: "hereby assigns all right, title and interest"

plainEnglish: Someone charges you to put your song on a playlist and promises a number of streams or followers. Many of these playlists are filled with bots or fake accounts.
whyItHurts: Streaming platforms can detect artificial streams. The result can be removed tracks, withheld royalties, a flagged artist profile, or your distributor dropping your account.
whatToDo: Pitch real curators directly and through your own artist dashboard instead.
Never pay anyone who guarantees a stream count or a placement.
If you already paid for one, stop and check your account for removal notices.
lookFor: "playlist submission fee" with a promised result

plainEnglish: Streams, saves or followers created by automated accounts or click farms, usually sold as a "growth service".
whyItHurts: Fake numbers do not turn into real fans. They distort your analytics, and platforms may penalize you or fine your distributor.
whatToDo: Judge a promoter by their method, not by promised totals.
Look for sudden spikes from one country or with no saves and no listener growth.
Report suspicious activity to your distributor right away.

plainEnglish: A distributor that looks cheap at signup but charges every year per release, so your music is taken down if you stop paying.
whyItHurts: Years later, a catalog of old releases can turn into a recurring bill, and a lapsed payment can pull the songs off streaming, breaking playlists and linked profile history.
whatToDo: Before uploading, find the distributor's fee page and check whether the cost is one-time, yearly per release, or a subscription.
Check what happens to your releases if you stop paying.
Keep a spreadsheet of every release and renewal date.

plainEnglish: An advance is a loan against your future royalties. Recoupment means you receive no royalties until the label earns back everything it spent. Cross-collateralization means losses on one record or cost are charged against earnings from others.
whyItHurts: You can have a hit and still receive nothing, because marketing, video and recording costs may all be treated as your debt.
whatToDo: Ask for a list of exactly which costs are recoupable.
Ask that each release stands alone for recoupment.
Ask for audit rights so you can verify statements.

plainEnglish: The company is legally treated as the author of your work from the moment you create it, as if you were an employee.
whyItHurts: You may lose ownership and statutory rights to reclaim copyrights later. It is often used to take songs or recordings outright.
whatToDo: Do not accept a work-for-hire term in a deal for your own songs or recordings unless you understand it.
Ask a lawyer whether it applies to what you are doing.
If you are the one hiring producers or engineers, use a clear agreement instead of relying on handshakes.

plainEnglish: A venue or promoter makes you buy tickets, bring a minimum number of paying people, or pay a fee for the chance to play or be "seen by industry".
whyItHurts: The only guaranteed beneficiary is the promoter. "Industry" attendees are often nonexistent.
whatToDo: Ask who will be there and what the promoter does to bring an audience.
Prefer shows where you get a door split or a guaranteed fee.
Check reviews from other artists before agreeing.
lookFor: "A&R will be attending" with no names

plainEnglish: A "label" asks you to pay for your own recording, marketing or "development" and then promises a deal or promotion.
whyItHurts: Real labels invest their own money. If you are paying for everything, you are the customer, and may also be signing away rights.
whatToDo: If you pay, treat it as a service purchase with a clear scope, deliverables and refund terms.
Make sure the deal does not also take ownership or a share of your income.
Search the company name plus "scam" or "complaints".

plainEnglish: A deal that quietly gives away part or all of your publishing, which is your songwriter income, when you only wanted a service such as collection or admin.
whyItHurts: Publishing income can last decades and is separate from the master. Giving it away early is hard to reverse.
whatToDo: Learn the difference between administration, where you keep ownership and pay a fee, and co-publishing, where you transfer part of it.
Ask exactly what is being transferred and for how long.
Get a lawyer to review any deal that mentions publishing.

plainEnglish: You can only release music through one company for a long time, and the company holds options to extend the deal on its own schedule. A re-record restriction stops you from remaking the songs later.
whyItHurts: If the company stops supporting you, you can still be stuck unable to release elsewhere for years.
whatToDo: Ask for a short initial term and limit the options.
Add a minimum release commitment so you are not stuck if they do nothing.
Check the re-record restriction length.

plainEnglish: A distribution agreement that makes it hard or impossible to remove your music, or keeps taking a share after you leave.
whyItHurts: A normal distribution agreement should be a service you can cancel. If you can't leave, you've lost control of your catalog.
whatToDo: Read the termination section before uploading.
Avoid any agreement where you cannot remove your music on notice.
Check if the distributor takes any ownership share.

plainEnglish: Letters or emails that look official and say you must pay to "register", "protect" or "claim" your music, or that unclaimed royalties are waiting for a fee.
whyItHurts: They imitate real institutions. Real collection societies and registries do not demand surprise payments by email.
whatToDo: Go to the official site yourself instead of using links in the message.
Compare the sender with the official contact details.
Never pay a fee to receive royalties.
